title: IF GOD KNEW THEY WOULD EAT THE FORBIDDEN FRUIT, WHY DID HE PUT THE TREE THERE?
paragraphs: IF GOD KNEW THEY WOULD EAT THE FORBIDDEN FRUIT, WHY DID HE PUT THE TREE THERE?
The heartbreaking mystery of Eden, the freedom God gave humanity, the lie that shattered paradise, and the Savior who walked into our ruin to bring us home.
There is a question buried in the opening pages of the Bible that has troubled believers, fascinated theologians, and quietly haunted people who have never dared to ask it inside a church.
If God already knew Adam and Eve would eat from the forbidden tree, why did He put it there in the first place?
Think about that.

God knew the serpent would deceive. He knew Eve would reach for the fruit. He knew Adam would eat. He knew shame would enter the human experience, that the ground would be cursed, that death would become humanity's enemy, and that generations yet unborn would inherit a world fractured by sin.
He knew there would be graves.
He knew there would be wars.

He knew there would be children crying beside hospital beds, marriages collapsing under betrayal, mothers burying sons, and people lying awake at three in the morning wondering why life hurts so much.
And still, in the middle of Eden, stood the tree.
Why?
Was it a trap?
Was God testing humanity with a test He already knew they would fail?
And if He knew everything that would happen, why didn't He simply create a garden without the possibility of disobedience?
Perhaps you've asked that question before. Perhaps someone told you to stop questioning God and just have faith.
But Scripture does not require us to pretend difficult questions are easy.
And the answer is far more profound than the familiar explanation that God simply wanted people to have free will.
Because when we examine Genesis carefully, something extraordinary begins to emerge.
The story of the forbidden tree is not merely about why humanity fell. It is also the beginning of the biblical story that leads us to the cross where Jesus Christ came to rescue the fallen.
But to understand that, we must return to the garden.
Before the shame.
Before the hiding.
Before the first human being ever learned what it meant to be afraid of the God who loved him.

Genesis 2:9 tells us that the LORD God caused trees to grow from the ground, trees that were beautiful to look at and good for food. Among them were the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
Notice something easily overlooked.
God did not create a barren prison and place one tempting fruit in front of two starving people.
He created abundance.
There were trees everywhere. Food everywhere. Beauty everywhere. Provision everywhere.
And then God gave a command.
In Genesis 2:16–17, the LORD told the man that he could freely eat from every tree of the garden except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Eating from that tree would bring death.
The original Hebrew contains a detail worth noticing.
The words translated "you may surely eat" are:
אָכֹל תֹּאכֵל — ʾākōl tōʾkēl
This construction repeats the Hebrew verb for eating to emphasize the certainty or freedom of the permission.
In natural English, the sense is, "You may freely eat."
Before God spoke about the one forbidden tree, He spoke about the many trees they could enjoy.
The first emphasis was generosity, not restriction.
That matters.
Because the serpent's strategy would be to make Adam and Eve forget the abundance and obsess over the boundary.
And isn't that still how temptation works?
You can have a hundred reasons to be grateful, yet one thing you cannot have begins consuming your thoughts.
You can have a loving family, yet someone else's attention starts feeling irresistible.
You can have blessings you once prayed for, yet comparison whispers that God has withheld the one thing that would finally make you happy.
Suddenly, everything God has given looks smaller than the thing He has forbidden.
The garden begins to feel like a prison.
And the boundary begins to look like cruelty.
But was the tree itself evil?
No.
Genesis calls it the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. It does not say the tree was inherently wicked, nor does it describe its fruit as poisonous.
In fact, Genesis 3:6 describes the tree as good for food, pleasing to the eyes, and desirable for gaining wisdom.
The danger was not that God had created an evil substance.
The danger was that human beings would cross a boundary God had established, choosing disobedience over trust.
The Hebrew name of the tree is especially important:
עֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע — ʿēṣ haddaʿat ṭôḇ wā-rāʿ
Literally, "the tree of the knowledge of good and evil."
The word דַּעַת — daʿat means knowledge.
But what exactly does "knowledge of good and evil" mean?

Christians have offered several interpretations. Some emphasize moral discernment, others the pursuit of wisdom apart from God's instruction, and others the human desire to claim authority over what is good and evil.
The phrase also appears elsewhere in the Old Testament in contexts involving discernment and maturity.
Genesis does not provide a complete philosophical definition.
But the serpent's promise reveals something central to the temptation.
"You will be like God," he tells the woman, "knowing good and evil" (Genesis 3:5).
The temptation was not simply to taste something delicious.
It was to reach for a godlike status on the serpent's terms.
To distrust the Creator.
To believe that God's command stood between humanity and something better.
To treat independence from God's word as the pathway to fullness of life.
And suddenly the question changes.
It is no longer only, "Why did God put the tree there?"
It becomes, "Why did humanity believe that disobeying the God who gave them everything would somehow give them more?"
That question is painfully personal.
Because we have been repeating the same tragedy ever since.
We know what Scripture says about forgiveness, but bitterness feels safer.
We know what Jesus teaches about truth, but a lie seems more convenient.
We know that sexual immorality damages lives, but desire promises satisfaction without consequences.
We know that greed cannot save us, but we keep believing one more possession will finally bring peace.
We know that pride destroys relationships, yet admitting we were wrong feels unbearable.
And then, when the consequences arrive, we ask why God allowed us to make the choice.
There is a little Eden in every human heart.
Not because we are personally responsible for Adam's individual decision, but because we recognize the same struggle between trusting God and believing we know better.
Yet the original question remains.
Why allow such a choice at all?
Here we must be careful.
A popular Christian answer says God placed the tree in Eden because genuine love requires free will.
There is something meaningful in that explanation. Scripture portrays Adam and Eve as morally responsible creatures who received a real command and were accountable for their disobedience.
But Genesis never explicitly says, "God planted this tree because love requires free will."
That is a theological inference, not a direct quotation from Scripture.
And thoughtful Christians have differed about how human freedom, divine sovereignty, and God's foreknowledge fit together.
What we can say with confidence is that God created humanity good, gave humanity a meaningful command, and did not portray disobedience as something He approved.
The tree marked a real distinction between the Creator and His creatures.
Adam and Eve were made in God's image, but they were not God.
They were given dignity, responsibility, fellowship, and extraordinary freedom.
Yet they were still called to trust the One who made them.
Being made in God's image never meant being entitled to take God's place.
And that is where the serpent attacked.
Genesis 3:1 records his opening question:
"Did God really say...?"
Those words should disturb us.
Because the first recorded temptation in Scripture begins by casting suspicion on what God has spoken.
The serpent did not begin by openly declaring war against heaven.
He began with a question designed to unsettle trust.
Then he contradicted God's warning.
"You will not surely die" (Genesis 3:4).
The Hebrew is emphatic:
לֹא־מוֹת תְּמֻתוּן — lōʾ-môt tĕmutûn
The serpent was directly denying the certainty of death.
God had warned that disobedience would bring death.
The serpent insisted it would not.
And the woman listened.
She saw that the tree was good for food, pleasing to the eyes, and desirable for wisdom.
She took.
She ate.
She gave some to her husband, who was with her.
And he ate.
No lightning is described striking the garden.
No dramatic explosion is recorded.
Just an act of disobedience.
A moment in which the word of the serpent was trusted above the word of God.
And then everything changed.
Genesis 3:7 says their eyes were opened, and they realized they were naked.
Before the fall, Genesis 2:25 says they were naked and unashamed.
Afterward, they covered themselves.
The people who had lived without shame were suddenly trying to hide their vulnerability.
And then came one of the most heartbreaking moments in the entire Bible.
They heard the LORD God in the garden.
And they hid.
Imagine that.
The very presence that should have been their greatest comfort had become the presence they feared.
Adam, formed from the dust by God's own creative power, was now hiding among the trees God had made.
And God called to him.
אַיֶּכָּה — ʾayyekkāh
"Where are you?" (Genesis 3:9).
Read those words slowly.
Where are you?
The text does not explain God's inner reason for asking, but the question clearly draws Adam into an encounter with the truth about what has happened.
The God who knows His creation calls the hiding man to answer.
And Adam replies that he was afraid because he was naked, so he hid.
There it is.
Fear.
Shame.
Concealment.
The human heart learning to run from God.
And if we're willing to be truthful, this is where Genesis stops feeling like ancient history.
Because some of us have been hiding for years.
Not behind fig leaves.
Behind a smile.
Behind church attendance.
Behind ministry involvement.
Behind carefully selected Bible verses posted online while our private lives are falling apart.
Behind the words, "I'm fine," when we know we are not.
Maybe you love Jesus, but there is a sin you keep returning to.
Maybe you have been wounded by someone who claimed to represent God.
Maybe your prayers have become shorter because guilt has convinced you that heaven is tired of hearing your voice.
Maybe you still attend worship, but something inside you feels distant.
And perhaps the hardest part is that you remember a time when being close to God felt easier.
Now you hide.
You distract yourself.
You promise to change.
You fail.
You feel ashamed.
And you hide again.
But listen carefully.
The God who confronted Adam's sin did not leave Adam hidden among the trees.
He called him into the open.
Not because sin was insignificant.
But because hiding was never going to heal what disobedience had broken.
You can simply write, "No more hiding," or "Pray for me."
You do not need to expose private details to strangers. But you do not have to keep pretending that the battle is not real.
Now comes the difficult part.
God had warned that eating from the tree would bring death.
And death did enter the human story.
Adam and Eve did not physically collapse the moment they ate. Genesis goes on to describe their continued lives outside Eden.
But the sentence of mortality was pronounced, and their access to the tree of life was barred.
Genesis 3:19 declares that humanity would return to the ground, for from dust human beings were taken, and to dust they would return.
Romans 5:12 later connects the entrance of sin and death into the human world with Adam's transgression.
The Bible does not treat the fall as a harmless mistake.
It treats it as a catastrophe.
The relationship between humanity and God was ruptured.
Human relationships were distorted.
The ground became a place of painful toil.
Death cast its shadow over human existence.
And the garden was lost.
So we must ask the question again.
If God knew this would happen, why did He not prevent it?
The most faithful answer begins with an admission that many of us find uncomfortable.
Scripture does not reveal every reason God permitted the fall.
It reveals enough for us to know that God is holy, that His creation was good, that human disobedience was real, and that He was not surprised or defeated by sin.
But it does not give us permission to invent a complete explanation of every mystery in God's eternal purposes.
Deuteronomy 29:29 reminds us that the secret things belong to the LORD, while what He has revealed belongs to His people.
That is not an invitation to abandon thought.
It is a reminder that there is a difference between trusting what God has revealed and claiming to know what He has not.
We must not say that God needed Adam and Eve to sin.
We must not say that evil is good because God can bring good from it.
We must not say that suffering is merely a tool God uses without regard for the people experiencing it.
And we must never suggest that the horrors of human history are somehow insignificant because redemption is possible.
Sin is evil.
Death is an enemy.
Suffering is real.
The tears matter.
But here is the astonishing testimony of Scripture.
God is able to bring redemption out of a rebellion He never commands us to commit.
The cross itself demonstrates this.
Acts 2:23 speaks of Jesus being delivered up according to God's definite plan and foreknowledge, while also holding those who crucified Him responsible for their wicked actions.
God's sovereign purpose did not turn human evil into righteousness.
And human evil did not overthrow God's saving purpose.
That distinction is essential.
Because otherwise we risk portraying God as the author of the very wickedness Scripture condemns.
But the biblical story shows something far greater.
A holy God who judges sin and, in astonishing mercy, acts to save sinners.
And the first glimpse of that mercy appears before Adam and Eve ever leave Eden.

In Genesis 3:15, God speaks to the serpent about enmity between the serpent's offspring and the woman's offspring, and about the conflict in which the serpent's head will be struck and the offspring's heel will be struck.
Christians have long recognized this passage as the first anticipation of the Gospel, often calling it the protoevangelium, or "first Gospel."
The Hebrew word for offspring is:
זֶרַע — zeraʿ
It can refer to seed, descendants, or offspring.
In its immediate context, Genesis 3:15 announces conflict between the serpent and the woman's offspring.
Read within the whole Christian canon, the promise finds its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the victorious offspring who defeats the works of the devil.
We should not pretend Adam and Eve necessarily understood every future detail of Christ's crucifixion.
The verse does not explicitly name Jesus or describe the nails of Calvary.
But the New Testament reveals the larger story into which this promise fits.
First John 3:8 declares that the Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the devil.
Hebrews 2:14–15 explains that through death Jesus defeated the one who held the power of death and delivered those enslaved by its fear.
And Romans 16:20 promises that the God of peace will crush Satan under the feet of His people.
What began in Eden was not going to have the final word.
The serpent would not reign forever.
Sin would not triumph forever.
Death would not hold God's redeemed people forever.
And the answer would not come through humanity somehow climbing its way back to innocence.
It would come through a Savior.
Where Adam disobeyed, Christ obeyed.
That is not merely a poetic comparison.
It is apostolic teaching.
Romans 5:19 declares that through the disobedience of the one man, many were made sinners, and through the obedience of the One, many will be made righteous.
First Corinthians 15:22 says that as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive, a statement Paul develops in the context of resurrection and belonging to Christ.
And First Corinthians 15:45 calls Jesus the last Adam.
Think about what that means.
The first Adam stood in a garden surrounded by provision and chose disobedience.
Jesus, the last Adam, entered a garden of anguish and submitted Himself to the Father's will.
In Gethsemane, with the suffering of the cross before Him, Jesus prayed:
"Not my will, but yours, be done" (Luke 22:42).
Adam grasped at what God had forbidden.
Christ surrendered Himself in obedience to the Father.
Adam's sin brought condemnation and death.
Christ's obedience, culminating in His sacrificial death and victorious resurrection, brings justification and life to those who belong to Him.
The contrast is breathtaking.
But do not miss the cost.
Jesus did not restore sinners by pretending sin did not matter.
He carried our sins.
He endured the cross.
He suffered under the weight of human cruelty and the judgment associated with our sin.
First Peter 2:24 says that He bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we might die to sins and live for righteousness.
The Greek word used there for tree or wood is:
ξύλον — xylon
The word can refer to wood, a tree, or a wooden instrument.
Peter uses it for the cross.
And the connection is deeply moving.
Humanity's rebellion involved a forbidden tree.
Our redemption was accomplished through the obedience of Christ, who bore our sins upon the wood of the cross.
This is a theological contrast drawn from the wider biblical story, not a claim that Genesis explicitly identifies the two trees as identical symbols.
But the connection calls us to worship.
The first Adam reached out his hand in disobedience.
Jesus stretched out His hands in sacrificial love.
And what humanity could never repair by its own righteousness, Christ accomplished through His death and resurrection.
The scandal of Eden was answered by the grace of Calvary.
This is why the Gospel is not merely advice for becoming a better person.
It is good news about what Jesus Christ has done for people who cannot save themselves.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes most personal.
Because the question, "Why did God put the tree there?" can sometimes conceal a second question.
One we are almost afraid to speak.
"Why did God allow me to become the person I am today?"
Why did He allow me to make those choices?
Why did He let me walk into that relationship?
Why didn't He stop me before I destroyed something precious?
Why didn't He intervene before my life became so complicated?
Those are painful questions.
And not every tragedy in your life is the result of your own sin. Scripture itself rejects simplistic explanations that blame every sufferer for the suffering they endure (John 9:1–3).
Some wounds were inflicted on you.
Some losses came without your choosing.
Some sorrows remain mysteries this side of eternity.
But where you have sinned, the Gospel offers something greater than excuses.
It offers forgiveness.
Where you have been wounded, it offers the presence and hope of the risen Christ, even when healing is slow.
Where you are ashamed, it calls you out of hiding.
Where you are enslaved by sin, it calls you to repentance and new life through the power of the Holy Spirit.
And where you have convinced yourself that your story is beyond repair, it points you to a crucified and risen Savior.
Not every consequence disappears when you repent.
Not every broken relationship is restored immediately.
Not every wound closes overnight.
But in Jesus Christ, sin does not have to remain your master.
And shame does not have to become your identity.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says that anyone in Christ is a new creation.
Not a person who never had a past.
A new creation.
Someone whose past no longer has the authority to define their standing before God.
That is grace.
Not permission to continue in sin.
Not denial of the damage sin causes.
Grace is God's undeserved favor in Christ, which forgives and transforms.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God brings salvation and trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
The same grace that welcomes the repentant sinner also teaches that sinner to walk away from the sin.
And that is why Jesus did not die merely to make us feel better about ourselves.
He died to reconcile us to God.
He rose again so that death would not be the end of the story.
And He calls us to follow Him.
Now look at the Bible's ending.
Because the story that begins with a tree in Genesis does not conclude with humanity permanently banished from God's presence.
In Revelation 22, the tree of life appears again.
Revelation 22:2 describes the tree of life in the New Jerusalem, and Revelation 22:3 declares that there will no longer be any curse.
Do you see the movement of the biblical story?
Genesis begins with humanity enjoying God's provision in a garden.
Sin brings exile, suffering, and death.
Christ comes, dies, and rises again.
And Revelation ends with God's redeemed people dwelling in His presence, with the curse removed.
The Bible does not end with Adam hiding.
It ends with God's servants seeing His face (Revelation 22:4).
The Hebrew Bible begins with the tragedy of humanity turning away from the Creator.
The Christian Scriptures conclude with the glorious hope of redeemed humanity living in the presence of God and the Lamb.
The tree of life, once inaccessible to fallen humanity, appears in the final vision of God's restored creation.
That is not a small ending.
That is cosmic redemption.
And the center of it all is Jesus.
Not human goodness.
Not religious performance.
Not an impressive ministry.
Not the ability to quote enough Bible verses to hide a wounded conscience.
Jesus Christ.
The Lamb who was slain.
The Savior who rose.
The King who will make all things new.
So what is the answer to our original question?
Why did God place the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in Eden when He knew Adam and Eve would eat from it?
Scripture shows that God created a good world, gave humanity abundant provision and a genuine command, and held humanity responsible for choosing disobedience.
It also shows that God's foreknowledge did not mean the fall took Him by surprise, and that His saving purpose in Christ would overcome the devastation of sin.
But Scripture does not reveal an exhaustive explanation of why God permitted this particular history rather than a different one.
We should be humble enough to admit that.
What Scripture does reveal is the character of the God who entered our broken history to redeem us.
We may not understand every reason He permitted the fall.
But we can look at the cross and see that He did not remain distant from the suffering of this fallen world.
In Jesus Christ, God the Son took on human nature and entered the world of grief, temptation, rejection, betrayal, suffering, and death.
Yet He was without sin.
He did not merely observe humanity's misery from heaven.
He came to save.
And the empty tomb declares that death itself will not have the final word.
Perhaps the deepest question is no longer why the tree was there.
Perhaps it is this:
Now that Christ has come to rescue sinners, what will you do with Him?
Will you continue hiding?
Will you keep telling yourself that you will repent when life becomes less complicated?
Will you wait until your habits improve before coming to the Savior who calls sinners to Himself?
Or will you finally admit that you need the mercy of God?
You do not need to manufacture a perfect testimony before you come to Jesus.
You need to turn to Him in repentance and faith.
Confess your sins.
Trust in His finished work, not your own righteousness.
Believe that He died for sins and rose again.
Follow Him.
And when you stumble, do not make hiding your home.
Return to the Savior.
First John 1:9 reminds believers that God is faithful and just to forgive confessed sins and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
That promise is not an excuse to cherish sin.
It is a reason to stop running from the One who saves.
And if you have been reading this with tears in your eyes because you recognize yourself in Adam's hiding, please hear this:
Your sin is serious.
But the mercy of Christ is greater than the hope you could ever build on your own goodness.
Your wounds are real.
But they do not place you beyond the compassion of the Savior.
Your past may contain chapters you wish you could erase.
But through Jesus Christ, your future does not have to be ruled by them.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not because the past never happened.
Not because consequences never matter.
But because redemption is real.
Because the cross is sufficient.
Because the tomb is empty.
Because Jesus Christ is alive.
And because the God who called to Adam in the garden still calls sinners through His Gospel to come out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
Write "No more hiding" if you are ready to stop running from God.
Write "Jesus, forgive me" if this has brought you to honest repentance.
Or write "Christ is still healing me" if you are learning to trust His grace in the middle of a difficult journey.
You can also share a testimony or ask for prayer without revealing anything you need to keep private.
Sometimes the courage to speak one honest sentence encourages another struggling believer to seek help, confess sin, and return to Christ.
And please, don't let this message end with you.
Someone may be angry with God.
Someone may be quietly questioning their faith.
Someone may be drowning in shame while pretending everything is fine.
Someone may have never understood why Jesus came.
We want to help people open their Bibles, ask honest questions, grow in discernment, and keep their eyes on Christ.
These resources are intended to help believers go deeper into Scripture, strengthen their understanding of the Gospel, and grow in their walk with Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry has blessed you, there is another way you can help carry the work forward.
But we want to be biblically clear about something important.
Scripture calls believers to give willingly, not under pressure or guilt.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that each person should give what they have decided in their heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Your prayers, thoughtful comments, sharing of Gospel-centered content, and encouragement to others also matter.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, conversation starters, or thoughtful gifts. But the greatest gift we could ever point you toward is not something sold in a store.
It is the grace of God in Jesus Christ.
We would be grateful to walk alongside you as we continue studying Scripture, confronting difficult questions, and encouraging one another to follow Jesus faithfully.
It is not to build a kingdom around a page.
It is to point people to the Kingdom of God.
It is not to make a name for ourselves.
It is to proclaim the name of Jesus Christ.
It is not to sell the appearance of spiritual transformation.
It is to bear witness to the Savior who truly transforms lives.
And now, before you go, I want you to picture something.
A man hiding among the trees in Eden.
Ashamed.
Afraid.
Unable to undo what he had done.
Then picture another scene.
A Savior hanging upon the wood of a cross.
Rejected.
Wounded.
Bearing sins that were not His own.
The first scene shows humanity's desperate need.
The second reveals God's astonishing answer.
And beyond the cross stands an empty tomb.
Beyond the tomb stands the promise of resurrection.
Beyond this broken age stands the hope of a new creation where the curse will be no more.
We began with a question about why God allowed a tree to stand in Eden.
We end with a Savior who willingly endured the cross to bring sinners back to God.
And perhaps the most unforgettable truth is not that Adam reached for what God had forbidden.
It is that, after humanity fell, God did not abandon His purpose to redeem.
The first Adam hid among the trees in shame. The last Adam bore our shame upon a tree, so that those who belong to Him could come home.
